name: Forest-tundra / krummholz
notes: Forest-tundra ecotone and treeline krummholz: wind-stunted conifers, dwarf birch/willow, heath and lichen mats. Drawn on Scandinavia/Siberia (birch-spruce), Rockies (spruce-fir) and Alps (mountain pine).

canopy.name: Lodgepole pine

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with 3-6 cotyledons and a tuft of single primary needles, then short, twisted, paired needles. Young trees are dense, narrow cones with regular whorls. Open-grown shore pines become bushy, crooked and flat-topped; inland trees become slim, straight poles. Serotinous cones stay closed on the branches for decades.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (Lotan & Critchfield): viable seed commonly at 5-10 years; ~3.6 m at 20 years on medium sites; germination peaks in the 2 weeks after snowmelt; very intolerant of shade; shore pine small and short-lived; ages commonly 150-200+, old high-elevation trees to 400+

canopy.source: western North American mountains; 20–35 m. Dense even-aged stands after fire; cones open in heat. Kew POWO for the name; standard floras for range.

canopy.silhouette: matted spruce skirt with a few flagged spires

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with 6-12 slender cotyledons; after 10 years often only 15-30 cm tall. Saplings are narrow, dense spires of sharp, square, blue-green needles. At treeline wind and snow shear them into flag trees (branches only on the lee side) or low krummholz mats that spread by branches rooting where they touch the ground.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (Alexander & Shepperd): seedlings 2.5 cm at 1 yr, 15-30 cm at 10, 1.2-1.5 m at ~20 yrs in sun; cones from 15-40 yrs, heavy crops at 150-250; dominants 250-450 yrs, 500-600 not rare; shade tolerant; dwarf layering form at timberline. Height-age fitted to the stunted 1-8 m form

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics (strobili break bud late April-May; pollen late May to early July by elevation; cones 2.5-6.3 cm mature in one season, ripen Aug-early Sep, open and shed seed Sep-Oct with some through winter); crop and decay estimated

canopy.name: Subalpine fir

growth.juvenile_note: Germinates on moist mineral soil or rotten wood just after snowmelt: 4-6 cotyledons, then short flat blue-green needles. Seedlings grow only a few centimetres a year in shade and make dense, narrow, spire-shaped young trees. At the treeline the young fir stays a low mat whose snow-buried branches root (layering), with a few wind-flagged stems poking above the snow.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (Alexander, Shearer & Shepperd): seed production begins at about 20 years, good crops every 3-5 years; seeds germinate soon after snowmelt; very tolerant of shade; trees rarely exceed 250 years; at timberline reproduces by layering and forms krummholz.

repro.note: at the treeline lower branches pressed down by snow take root (layering), which here plays the runner's part

canopy.source: Abies lasiocarpa, subalpine fir: Yukon and SE Alaska to Arizona and New Mexico; with Engelmann spruce the forming tree of the Rocky Mountain spruce-fir treeline; 15-30 m in subalpine forest, a wind-shorn mat with flagged spires at its upper limit. Kew POWO; USDA Silvics; Arno & Hammerly 1984 Timberline.

canopy.name: Mountain hemlock

growth.juvenile_note: Germinates on rotten wood, moss or mineral soil after the snow goes: 3-4 cotyledons, then short, soft, blue-green needles set all round the twig. Saplings grow slowly (often only a few cm a year under snowpack) into a narrow cone whose leader droops at the tip. At the treeline it stays a sprawling shrub whose snow-pressed branches root.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (Means): very slow early growth; seed crops from about 20 years (estimated from the silvics range); old trees commonly 400-800 years; tolerant of shade; krummholz and layering at timberline.

repro.note: at the treeline snow-pressed lower branches take root (layering), which here plays the runner's part

canopy.name: Whitebark pine

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings come up in clusters from the seed caches of Clark's nutcrackers, often a year or two after caching: 7-11 cotyledons, then single primary needles, then bundles of five stout yellow-green needles. Growth is very slow; clusters grow into several-stemmed trees, and at the treeline into low, sprawling krummholz with white-grey bark.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (Arno & Hoff): seeds largely dispersed and planted by Clark's nutcracker, germination often delayed one or more years; cone-bearing begins at 20-30 years, large crops at 60-80; very slow growth; ages commonly over 500 years, to about 1,000+

shrub.name: Alpenrose

growth.juvenile_note: Minute seedlings on moss or raw humus: two tiny cotyledons, then small glossy, dark green, leathery leaves with rusty-brown scaly undersides and rolled edges. For years it is a small, few-stemmed sprig; then it branches densely into a low, rounded evergreen bush, and stems that touch the ground root and spread it into a clonal patch.
growth.source: German Wikipedia Rostblaettrige Alpenrose (30-130 cm; stems 1-2 cm thick nearly 100 yr old; leaves live ~2 yr; flowers May-Jul, corolla to 2 cm, deep pink to red; capsules to 7 mm ripen from August; semi-shade light value; 440-2,840 m); germination and first flowering estimated

shrub.name: Green alder

growth.juvenile_note: Tiny winged nutlets germinate on bare moist mineral soil (avalanche tracks, landslides, moraine). The seedling makes a whip with small, sticky, toothed leaves, then sprouts several stems from the base. Snow presses the stems downslope every winter, so the shrub grows as a thicket of arching, elbowed stems that curve up at the tips.
growth.source: Flora Europaea and Flora of North America Alnus viridis / A. alnobetula (shrub 1-5 m, rarely more; leaves sticky, doubly serrate; catkins with the leaves; N-fixing with Frankia; pioneer of avalanche tracks and treeline). Germination, first fruit and age estimated.

Kew POWO; Flora Europaea; Flora of North America; Ellenberg 1988 (Alnetum viridis).

ground.name: Feather moss

growth.juvenile_note: A spore germinates into a green, thread-like protonema on humus or rotten wood that buds small leafy shoots. These become loose, glossy yellow-green, once-pinnate feathery shoots on conspicuous red stems with blunt, crowded leaves, adding roughly 1-2 cm a year and weaving into a springy carpet 3-10 cm deep. Most new patches start from broken shoot fragments.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Pleurozium schreberi (stems 6-15 cm; spores shed 9-12 months after fertilization; post-fire cover ~1% at 5 yr, 3% at 20-30 yr, 9% at 50 yr: decades to recover). Annual shoot growth (~1-2 cm/yr), patch size-age and lifespan estimated from feathermoss literature.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.name: Stair-step moss

growth.juvenile_note: Young plants are small loose wefts of red-stemmed, feathery, olive to golden-green fronds creeping over humus, logs or rock. Each year a new frond arches up from the middle of last year's, so a shoot becomes a staircase of flat, fern-like steps, one per year, the oldest dying brown underneath. A deep carpet rebuilds only slowly after fire, once a canopy has closed.
growth.source: Trees for Life (new segment each year from the centre of the previous one, segments live up to ~8 yr, sporophytes uncommon, slow recolonisation after fire, shade-loving); Wikipedia (one step per year used to age shoots). Lifespan is for the patch; spore-to-plant time and first capsule age estimated.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.name: Conifer coral

repro.note: The mycelium is the organism and lives in the substrate for years; the mushroom is a days-long fruiting body. 'rhizome' here = the mycelium spreading through the soil or litter; 'wind' = spores.

ground.source: Phaeoclavulina abietina (Pers.) Giachini (syn. Ramaria abietina, Mike's binomial), green-staining coral: Europe and North America in needle litter under spruce and fir; a small ochre to olive coral 2-7 cm that bruises green. Index Fungorum; Funga Nordica.

traits.native_range: needle litter under spruce and fir

cap.form: small coral 2-7 cm tall, a short base dividing into many upright forked branches with pointed tips
cap.notes: ochre to olive-ochre branches that bruise and age blue-green; white mycelium binds the needles at the base

epiphyte.name: Witch's hair lichen

growth.juvenile_note: New thalli start from fragments blown or dropped onto conifer twigs. A young thallus is a small erect pale tuft; as it lengthens it bends over and hangs as a loose beard of branched, pale yellow-green to grey-green strands, flecked with tiny white streaks, growing a few centimetres a year in humid subalpine air.
growth.source: Brodo, Sharnoff & Sharnoff 2001 Lichens of North America (Alectoria sarmentosa: pendent, 10-30 cm or more, pale yellowish-green, with conspicuous white elongate pseudocyphellae; on conifers in humid subalpine and boreal forest); Stevenson & Coxson growth studies (a few cm a year); ages estimated.

repro.note: a lichen: spreads almost entirely by fragments, carried by wind and nesting birds; no flowers

epiphyte.source: Alectoria sarmentosa, witch's hair: oceanic boreal and subalpine conifer forest, Cascades, Coast Mountains, interior Rockies, Scandinavia and the Alps; pale yellow-green hair lichen hanging 10-30 cm from spruce and fir branches; caribou winter forage. Brodo et al. 2001; Index Fungorum.

epiphyte.name: Beard lichen
epiphyte.source: Usnea barbata, beard lichen, cosmopolitan in humid montane forest, pale grey-green tufts hanging from twigs 10-50 cm — Wikipedia

traits.native_range: Usnea barbata, beard lichen, cosmopolitan in humid montane forest, pale grey-green tufts hanging from twigs 10-50 cm — W
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

epiphyte.silhouette: short pale lichen beards on twigs

growth.juvenile_note: Soredia or broken bits lodge on twigs and bark and grow into a tiny pale grey-green tuft a few mm tall, fixed by a blackened basal holdfast. Young thalli are shrubby and upright with short side fibrils; as they lengthen they bend over and hang as a beard of stringy, branched strands, each with a stretchy white central cord that shows when a strand is gently pulled apart.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Usnea): thalli from a few mm in polluted air to over 3 m, spread by fragments, soredia or isidia and by spores, very sensitive to sulphur dioxide, slow-growing in nature. Growth (on the order of 1 cm a year), establishment and ages estimated from pendulous beard lichens.
